case_title: V.P. Shrivastava v. Indian Explosives Ltd. & Ors.
accused_occupation: Senior employees of Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited (FCIL), a government company; both availed the Voluntary Suppression Scheme and were discharged
accused_victim_relationship: Business counterparty: the accused were senior employees of supplier FCIL, which had a tripartite supply arrangement with the complainant company Indian Explosives Ltd. (IEL)
offence_category: Cheating/Fraud (as alleged by IEL; the Court held no offence of cheating was made out)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420 (cheating), s.406 (criminal breach of trust), s.120B (criminal conspiracy); complaint also invoked Companies Act 1956 ss.540 and 542
evidence_type: No trial evidence; the Court examined only the complaint's allegations and averments in IEL's civil suit plaint
trial_court_outcome: Magistrate took cognizance of the private complaint and issued summons; no trial verdict (pre-trial stage)
high_court_outcome: Petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed (complaint not quashed)
neutral_facts: The complainant is a company that manufactures and sells industrial explosives and obtained ammonium nitrate, a major raw material, from a supplier company. Under a tripartite arrangement with the supplier and a coal company, the complainant was to pay an equivalent value to the coal company, which would supply coal to the supplier, and the supplier would supply ammonium nitrate to the complainant. The supplier supplied ammonium nitrate for some time, then stopped because of a breakdown of a gas compressor and financial difficulties. The supplier had earlier been declared a sick company, and its winding up was under consideration by the relevant authority. The complainant alleges that the accused, who were senior employees of the supplier, deliberately concealed this status and the supplier's large dues to other creditors. It alleges that this induced the complainant to pay about Rs. 4.20 crore to the coal company between September and November 2001, without receiving ammonium nitrate in return. The complaint also alleges collusion between the accused. The material relied on is the complaint and the averments in the complainant's civil suit plaint against the supplier.
financial_property_loss: Rs. 4,20,41,622 (alleged payment to BCCL, as alleged by complainant)
premeditation_planning: Not found: the Court held no dishonest intention at the inception of the agreement could be inferred
motive: alleged: to induce IEL to enter into the tripartite agreement and part with money by suppressing the supplier's sick status
key_evidence_accepted: None as trial evidence; the Court relied on the complaint's own averments and the plaint in the civil suit
trial_duration: offence: not given (agreement entered 'some time in the year 2001'); trial judgment: not given (complaint filed 22 May 2003; cognizance order 30 October 2003); High Court: 28 February 2007; Supreme Court: 24 September 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Mr. Jaideep Gupta, senior counsel (with others listed). Respondent IEL: Mr. Sanjoy Ghosh. State counsel: Not stated
investigation_status: Private complaint filed; no police investigation referred to; magistrate took cognizance and issued summons
appeal_history: Trial court (Magistrate): cognizance taken and summons issued. High Court: s.482 petition dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, High Court order set aside, complaint quashed
prosecution_argument: Complainant (IEL) argued the accused suppressed FCIL's sick status to induce the agreement, amounting to cheating and criminal breach of trust (ss.415, 405 IPC); trial should decide truth of allegations
defence_argument: Complaint lacks ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust; no averment of dishonest intention or entrustment; complainant knew FCIL's financial health; dispute is civil and the complaint is mala fide
legal_principle_applied: Cheating requires fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of the inducement; later failure to perform is not enough. Criminal breach of trust requires entrustment. s.482 CrPC may quash a complaint that does not disclose the offence on its face
precedent_relied_upon: Ram Jas v. State of UP (1970) 2 SCC 740; Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168; S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar (2002) 1 SCC 241; Kuriachan Chacko v. State of Kerala (2008) 8 SCC 708; Medchl Chemicals v. Biological E (2000) 3 SCC 269; Hira Lal Hari Lal Bhagwati v. CBI (2003) 5 SCC 257; Anil Mahajan v. Bhor Industries (2005) 10 SCC 228; R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab AIR 1960 SC 866; Dinesh Dutt Joshi v. State of Rajasthan (2001) 8 SCC 570; G. Sagar Suri v. State of UP (2000) 2 SCC 636; Onkar Nath Mishra v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2008) 2 SCC 561; Common Cause v. Union of India (1999) 6 SCC 667; Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney v. State of Bombay AIR 1956 SC 575; Indian Oil Corpn. v. NEPC India Ltd. (2006) 6 SCC 736; All Cargo Movers v. Dhanesh Badarmal Jain (2007) 14 SCC 776
